properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-09-26, from the dev_reflow2 hub, looking at hubs "from a tiered system of systems approach, which often correlates to how an organization is structured", and bringing in Conway's Law: "organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations" (Melvin Conway, 1967; also the "mirroring hypothesis"). And its counter-move, the Reverse Conway Maneuver: determine the ideal architecture of the product first, then structure the teams to match. His tiers: "Each level could correspond to a organizational level. Say at the systems-of-systems level, you have a chief technology officer…"

WHY IT IS ITS OWN QUESTION: dec:idea-a-graph-whose-children-are-themselves-reflow2-designs named, on 09-22, that the ASSEMBLY ladder (part of) and the AUTHORITY ladder (answerable to) look identical written down and are different relations. Conway's Law says they converge whether anyone intends it or not; Reverse Conway says which should lead. A design tool that holds both ladders can do something neither an org chart nor a parts list can: say where they disagree.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN:
(a) TIERS FOLLOW THE ORG CHART. Each hub is a team or an office; the design is arranged by who answers to whom. What Conway's Law says happens anyway, and the easiest to set up.
(b) TIERS FOLLOW THE PRODUCT'S ASSEMBLY, AND PEOPLE ATTACH TO TIERS AS OWNERS (the Reverse Conway Maneuver). The engine hub exists because the engine is a thing; whoever owns it is recorded on it, and an org change moves owners, not the design.
(c) RECORD BOTH AND REPORT WHERE THEY DIVERGE — a Conway check. For example: an interface whose two sides are owned by people with no common owner below the top tier (Conway's "if two teams don't speak, their modules struggle to integrate", as a finding before it happens); or one owner holding designs from assemblies that never meet. The agent's extension of Anthony's point, not his words.

CHEAP OR EXPENSIVE, as far as known: (b) costs nothing new: ownership per design or node is already expressible (owned_by; req:a-node-can-say-who-may-change-it asks for the per-node form). (c) inside one design is a small detector once interfaces carry both sides and owners are recorded. Across designs it needs the tier machinery, which is the large part (dec:idea-a-top-level-graph-holds-what-the-component-graphs-share). (a) is cheap to set up and expensive later: an org change then means re-cutting the design.

COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, RECORDED BESIDE IT:
· A DESIGN TOOL SHOULD NOT PRESCRIBE AN ORG CHART. (c) must report, never judge (dec:report-dont-judge). A divergence may be deliberate, e.g. a platform team owning parts of every assembly.
· OWNERSHIP DATA IS THIN TODAY. Most designs name one owner for everything, so a Conway check would have little to read until owners are recorded per design or per part.
· THE LADDERS MAY NOT EVEN HAVE THE SAME SHAPE. One component can sit under several assemblies (the graph-not-tree point on the neighbouring node), while an org chart is usually a tree. That mismatch is itself the most common Conway finding.
properties.name: OPEN — should the tiers of a family of designs follow the product's assembly or the organization's structure (Conway's Law, and the Reverse Conway Maneuver), and should reflow2 read the two against each other and say where they diverge?
